```{python}
import polars as pl
import numpy as np
from lets_plot import *
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn import metrics
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

LetsPlot.setup_html(isolated_frame=True)

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/byuidatascience/data4dwellings/master/data-raw/dwellings_ml/dwellings_ml.csv"
df = pl.read_csv(url)

df_plot = df.with_columns(
    pl.col("before1980").cast(pl.Utf8).replace({"1": "Before 1980", "0": "1980 or After"}).alias("era")
)

# build and fit the same model from Task 1
features = df.drop(["parcel", "yrbuilt", "before1980"])
feature_names = features.columns

X = features.to_numpy()
y = df["before1980"].to_numpy()

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

clf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=150, random_state=42)
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred = clf.predict(X_test)
```


## QUESTION 1

1. __Describe the quality of your classification model using 2-3 different evaluation metrics.__ You also need to explain how to define/interpret each of the evaluation metrics you use.

I used three metrics to check how well the model is doing. Accuracy is just the percent of predictions that were right — ours is around 93%. Precision tells you how often the model is right when it says "before 1980", and recall tells you how many of the actual pre-1980 homes it caught. Recall matters more here because missing one of those homes is a bigger deal than a false alarm. The confusion matrix just shows all four outcomes (right/wrong for each class) in a grid so you can see exactly where errors are happening.

```{python}
accuracy = metrics.accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)
print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy:.4f} ({accuracy*100:.2f}%)\n")

report = metrics.classification_report(y_test, y_pred, target_names=["1980 or After", "Before 1980"], output_dict=True)
print("Classification Report:")
print(f"{'':>15} {'precision':>10} {'recall':>8}")
for label in ["1980 or After", "Before 1980"]:
    p = report[label]["precision"]
    r = report[label]["recall"]
    print(f"{label:>15} {p:>10.2f} {r:>8.2f}")

cm = metrics.confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)
print("Confusion Matrix:")
print(cm)
```

```{python}
# visualize the confusion matrix
cm_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "Actual": ["1980 or After", "1980 or After", "Before 1980", "Before 1980"],
    "Predicted": ["1980 or After", "Before 1980", "1980 or After", "Before 1980"],
    "Count": [int(cm[0, 0]), int(cm[0, 1]), int(cm[1, 0]), int(cm[1, 1])]
})

(
    ggplot(cm_df, aes(x="Predicted", y="Actual", fill="Count"))
    + geom_tile()
    + geom_text(aes(label="Count"), color="white", size=14)
    + scale_fill_gradient(low="#4393c3", high="#08306b")
    + labs(title="Confusion Matrix", x="Predicted", y="Actual")
    + theme_light()
)
```


## QUESTION 2

1. __Justify your classification model by discussing the most important features selected by your model.__ This discussion should include a plot of permutation importance values for the most important features. Were there any features you thought would be importance but weren't?

I used permutation importance, which works by shuffling one feature at a time and seeing how much the accuracy drops. The top three ended up being `livearea`, `sprice`, and `arcstyle_ONE-STORY`, which is pretty much what I guessed in Task 1. I thought `basement` and the garage columns might matter more than they did, but they were near the bottom — the model mostly just needed size and price to figure it out.

```{python}
# permutation importance on the test set
perm = permutation_importance(clf, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=10, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)

perm_df = (
    pl.DataFrame({
        "feature": feature_names,
        "importance": perm.importances_mean.tolist()
    })
    .sort("importance", descending=True)
    .head(15)
)

(
    ggplot(perm_df, aes(x="importance", y="feature"))
    + geom_bar(stat="identity", fill="#4393c3")
    + labs(title="Top 15 Features by Permutation Importance", x="Mean Accuracy Drop", y="Feature")
    + theme_light()
)
```

## QUESTION 3

1. __For the 3 most important features, explain their relationship to the target variable. Use a plot to illustrate the relationship.__ (3 plots minimum)

The top three features were `livearea`, `sprice`, and `arcstyle_ONE-STORY`. For living area, older homes are almost all on the smaller end — once you get above 2500 sq ft it's mostly post-1980. Sale price follows the same pattern since smaller homes sell for less. The one-story thing surprised me a little but makes sense — ranch-style homes were really common before 1980 and the charts show a clear difference between the two groups.

```{python}
# Plot 1: living area vs era
livearea_counts = (
    df_plot
    .filter(pl.col("livearea") <= 4000)
    .with_columns(
        pl.col("livearea")
        .cut([1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000], labels=["<1000", "1000-1500", "1500-2000", "2000-2500", "2500-3000", ">3000"])
        .alias("livearea_bin")
    )
    .group_by(["livearea_bin", "era"])
    .agg(pl.len().alias("count"))
    .sort("livearea_bin")
)

(
    ggplot(livearea_counts, aes(x="livearea_bin", y="count", fill="era"))
    + geom_bar(stat="identity", position="fill")
    + scale_fill_manual(values=["#4393c3", "#d6604d"])
    + labs(title="Living Area vs Era", x="Living Area (sq ft)", y="Proportion", fill="Era")
    + theme_light()
    + theme(legend_position="bottom")
)
```

```{python}
# Plot 2: sale price vs era
sprice_counts = (
    df_plot
    .filter(pl.col("sprice") <= 600000)
    .with_columns(
        pl.col("sprice")
        .cut([100000, 200000, 300000, 400000, 500000], labels=["<100k", "100-200k", "200-300k", "300-400k", "400-500k", ">500k"])
        .alias("sprice_bin")
    )
    .group_by(["sprice_bin", "era"])
    .agg(pl.len().alias("count"))
    .sort("sprice_bin")
)

(
    ggplot(sprice_counts, aes(x="sprice_bin", y="count", fill="era"))
    + geom_bar(stat="identity", position="fill")
    + scale_fill_manual(values=["#4393c3", "#d6604d"])
    + labs(title="Sale Price vs Era", x="Sale Price", y="Proportion", fill="Era")

```

```{python}
# Plot 3: one-story architectural style vs era
# arcstyle_ONE-STORY is a binary dummy column (1 = one-story, 0 = not)
one_story_counts = (
    df_plot
    .with_columns(
        pl.col("arcstyle_ONE-STORY").cast(pl.Utf8).replace({"1": "One-Story", "0": "Other Style"}).alias("style")
    )
    .group_by(["style", "era"])
    .agg(pl.len().alias("count"))
    .sort("style")
)

(
    ggplot(one_story_counts, aes(x="style", y="count", fill="era"))
    + geom_bar(stat="identity", position="fill")
    + scale_fill_manual(values=["#4393c3", "#d6604d"])
    + labs(title="Architectural Style (One-Story) vs Era", x="Architectural Style", y="Proportion", fill="Era")
    + theme_light()
    + theme(legend_position="bottom")
)
```
